title: One number and its four checks
intro: The summary named the score and listed what was done with it. This level gives the arithmetic that produces it, the sampling design behind the comparison with an independent method, and the two manipulations that move it, then reads the panel that sets evaluation transcripts against real traffic and says what the four checks together do and do not establish.

chapters.title: The difference of log-probabilities
chapters.body:
The quantity is defined one token position at a time, and the arithmetic behind it is short enough to walk through.

At a position and a layer, the [[j-lens-readout]] produces a distribution over the entire vocabulary. The activation in the [[residual-stream]] is multiplied by that layer's averaged Jacobian, passed through the [[unembedding-matrix]], and softmaxed. The [[jacobian-lens]] therefore supplies a number for every token the model could say. The score reads exactly one hundred and two of those numbers.

Two of them belong to the target words, fictional and simulation. Their log-probabilities are averaged. The other hundred belong to the control nouns — recipe, bicycl, guitar and ninety-seven more common concrete words with no bearing on artificiality. Those log-probabilities are averaged too, and that mean is subtracted from the first.

The subtraction does real work. The overall level of the readout varies from position to position: at some the lens spreads its mass across ordinary content words, at others it concentrates. The controls absorb that level. What remains reflects the two target words rather than how peaked the readout happened to be. A unit of the resulting score is a difference in lens log-probability and nothing more interpretable than that.

The last step averages the difference across the [[workspace-layers]]. The [[layer-bands]] result licenses the choice: the J-space is nearly empty over roughly the first third of depth and turns into output-shaped content late, so only the middle band is expected to carry the model's reading of the situation.

The cost of the collapse is visible in the construction. A [[j-lens-vector]] exists for every token and the readout ranks them all; the score fixes two in advance and discards the ranking. Measuring [[evaluation-awareness]] this way commits to the guess that those two words are where it shows.

The paper offers the classifier as a proof of concept and names its weak point itself. The word fictional can reach the lens during a genuine discussion of works of fiction, and no filter was applied to catch that.

chapters.title: Checked against a second method
chapters.body:
Nothing in the definition guarantees that the number tracks recognition of being tested. The first check compares it against a readout built on different machinery.

A [[natural-language-autoencoder]] has two stages. A verbalizer decodes an activation into a short text description, and a reconstructor, trained alongside the verbalizer, has to rebuild the activation from that text. An [[llm-grader]] then reads the description against a rubric. Prior work used the pipeline to detect [[latent-eval-awareness]]: positions where the decoded description asserts that the situation is a test while the model's own output says nothing of the kind. That is deliberately not [[verbalized-eval-awareness]], which can be counted straight off the transcript.

Both methods were run over one corpus. The transcripts come from automated auditing of Opus 4.6, a production model in the [[claude-model-family]], produced by the kind of investigator setup described under [[automated-auditing-agent]]. Every Assistant-turn-start position was scored, roughly 94,000 of them; [[readout-positions]] is the paper's separate treatment of why the start of a turn is where the lens gets read. The autoencoder pipeline flags 198, which is 0.2 percent.

That base rate forces the sampling design. A few hundred positions drawn uniformly would contain almost no flagged ones, so the comparison uses a stratified subset: all 198 flagged positions plus 594 drawn from the remainder, 792 in total.

On that subset the score reaches an [[auc]] of 0.853 against the autoencoder's verdicts, shown top left in [[fig-82]]. A randomly chosen flagged position outranks a randomly chosen unflagged one about 85 percent of the time, where 0.5 would be chance.

Two limits follow from the design. The verdicts are another method's output rather than ground truth, so what the number establishes is agreement between two readouts. And AUC is a ranking statistic computed on a re-balanced sample; it says nothing about how many positions above a chosen threshold in the full 94,000 would turn out to be flagged ones.

chapters.title: Moving the score from inside and from outside
chapters.body:
Agreeing with another method does not show that the score responds to the thing itself. Two further checks move something and watch the number follow. Both reuse transcripts and suites from the autoencoder study, which had already run them for its own measurements.

The first moves the model's state. A direction is derived from contrastive pairs of prompts that frame identical content once as a test and once as an ordinary conversation. That direction is added during generation, in the way [[steering-vectors]] are generally applied. It is not [[j-lens-steering]], which writes along lens directions, and it is not constrained to lie in the [[j-space]]; it was derived without reference to the lens at all. Neither is it [[eval-awareness-ablation]], which removed lens directions rather than adding anything.

Three strengths were used: $-0.1$ toward ordinary conversation, $0$, and $+0.1$ toward test. The model completed six evaluation suites at each setting. The score was computed at random positions within each response, around fifty scored positions per transcript. Under [[contrastive-eval-awareness-steering]] the mean rose monotonically with strength on every one of the six suites, top middle in the figure, with error bars giving standard errors over transcripts.

The second check moves the input instead. [[realism-edits]] rewrite an evaluation prompt so that the task survives but the surface tells of artificiality do not, leaving something that reads like real usage. Eleven suites were used, each original paired with its rewrite.

The rewrites lowered the mean score on all eleven suites. On eight of them the 95 percent confidence interval on the paired difference excludes zero, shown top right; on the remaining three it does not. The score falls without going to the deployment level, which matches the autoencoder study's finding that realism edits reduce the model's recognition of being evaluated rather than removing it.

chapters.title: Evaluations against real traffic
chapters.body:
The three checks so far all run inside evaluation data. The fourth asks whether the score separates evaluations from ordinary use.

Sixteen evaluation sets were drawn from the pre-release audits that [[alignment-auditing]] describes: seven alignment evaluations and nine capability evaluations. Against them stand two deployment controls, internal Claude.ai conversations and internal Claude Code sessions. Scores are aggregated per transcript, and the bottom panel draws a distribution for each set with a horizontal bar at its mean.

The deployment distributions center near 1.0. The four highest-scoring suites — Sycophancy, Appropriate Harmlessness, Blackmail, BrowseComp — sit two to three units above that, a unit being the difference in lens log-probability defined earlier.

The counts matter more than the extremes. Twelve of the sixteen evaluations score above the Claude Code sessions, and ten score above the Claude.ai conversations. Four therefore fail to clear the Claude Code baseline, and six fail to clear the Claude.ai one. [[deployment-vs-evaluation-comparison]] is a shift in distribution rather than a split, and no threshold on this axis separates the two kinds of transcript cleanly.

Taken together the four panels support something narrower than a detector. The score agrees with an independent readout, it moves when the model is pushed, it falls when the tells are removed, and it runs higher on tests than on use. Every one of those validations was borrowed from the autoencoder study rather than designed here. That is what makes the comparison tight, and it also means the score has not been asked anything the earlier study did not already ask.

The direction of the result lines up with [[eval-awareness-inhibits-misalignment]], the prior finding that a model which suspects a test behaves better than it otherwise would. A different limit sits underneath the whole measurement. [[selectivity]] means that what never enters the workspace is not there to be read, and [[automatic-misalignment-blind-spot]] names the case that matters: a behavior practiced enough to run without the workspace would leave this score nothing to find.
